Electrify America just opened its biggest charging station yet, with 24 DC fast chargers.
The new station is in Orlando, at Sand Lake Corners South shopping center on South John Young Parkway. Each of its 24 chargers can deliver up to 350 kW.
A 24-charger station gives a busy destination like Orlando more room to accommodate both everyday charging and vacation traffic.
The location puts drivers within reach of Interstate 4, Orlando International Airport, Walt Disney World, and Universal Studios. And because it’s in a shopping center, there are places to grab something to eat or run errands while charging.

Florida is a pretty logical place for Electrify America to go bigger. The state had roughly 450,400 registered battery electric vehicles in 2025, according to the US Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center . That’s the second-largest total in the US, behind California. Those figures count fully electric vehicles separately from plug-in hybrids.
All 24 chargers at Sand Lake Corners South feature CCS plugs only. Electrify America is also piloting NACS connectors at selected stations, including a separate location at the Florida Mall in Orlando. Drivers can check connector availability in the Electrify America app.
Electrify America says it now operates more than 350 chargers at over 60 stations in Florida. Another Orlando site, with 10 chargers at 10226 Curry Ford Road, is expected to open in the coming months, although the company hasn’t announced a specific opening date.

An MH-60R Seahawk lands on the flight deck aboard Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Gonzalez (DDG 66), Oct. 18, 2026. Gonzalez is deployed to the U.S. 5th Fleet area of operations to support maritime security and stability in the Middle East. (US Navy photo)
WASHINGTON — As Pentagon leaders remain tightlipped about the extent of damage to US bases in the Middle East, a senior US defense official said the administration is weighing possible force posture changes against costs as it decides which installations to rebuild.
“We’re meeting with CENTCOM [US Central Command] and doing the assessments right now from an installation perspective,” the senior defense official told reporters today at a Defense Writers Group breakfast. “Part of this is what will the global posture be in the future, and what does that require us to have?
The official added that the department is taking a strategic approach to investments, prioritizing where its presence is needed most.
After the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, Tehran and its proxies began targeting US bases in the region — including Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, where strikes rendered the Pentagon’s Combined Air Operations Center (COAC) inoperable , as well as other installations in Saudi Arabia and Jordan.
The US Navy’s Fifth Fleet was previously headquartered at Naval Support Activity Bahrain. But in an interview with The Epoch Times , Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao acknowledged that “they blew the hell out of Bahrain.” Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle separately said the Navy would not be using Naval Support Activity Bahrain “anytime soon.”
Pentagon leaders have provided lawmakers with cost estimates for the war with Iran, but those figures have not included a complete account of the costs associated with repairing US bases in the region. Earlier this week, members of the Senate Armed Services Committee called on the department to publicly disclose the total cost of the war in Iran, including damage to those US installations.
The senior defense official said they did not have a cost estimate readily available but that the department was taking a strategic approach to repairs. “It’s part of the reason we want to build a new base differently … nothing’s a sanctuary anymore,” the official said.
“The idea that we still have two oceans that keep any bad things from happening to us, that’s no longer a thing, so we’ve got to think differently. … The installation is the weapon system, and I have to have a mindset that I treat it like it’s a weapon system, not just a piece of real estate,” the official later added.
The proliferation of drones and cruise missiles presents another challenge, forcing the Pentagon to consider not only how to harden bases overseas but also how to protect installations on the US mainland, including through a diverse array of defense systems.
“I can’t pour four [feet] of concrete over everything, so I have to have a different approach, investments and strategies that we want to have in terms of how we make bases resilient, how I make them defensible, how I protect our people — all of that are things that we’re working on right now to come up with a different strategy,” the senior defense official said.
Part of that effort involves strengthening protection at individual bases, as well as working with the Golden Dome team to prioritize which locations to protect first and keep “risk as low as possible.”

Freight broker Fura announced it has acquired truckload brokerage Road Dog Logistics, adding approximately $30 million in revenue to Fura’s platform.
This is Frisco, Texas-based Fura’s eighth acquisition, meaningfully expanding its over $100-million AI-powered platform. Fura targets brokers with less than $30 million in annual revenue , a segment of the 3PL market that is often ignored by private equity.
Financial terms of the transaction were not provided.
Cincinnati-based Road Dog’s team will continue to manage daily operations, but will soon operate on Fura’s tech platform, which provides AI quoting, carrier-sales functions and shipment visibility.
“Road Dog is exactly the kind of company we want to fold into the platform: great brokers, loyal customers and a reputation for showing up,” said Jeff Dangelo, co-founder and CEO of Fura. “Our job now is to give that team better tools and more support, so they can spend their time growing the business instead of chasing paperwork.”
The deal deepens Fura’s reach in managed transportation and gives it a food-and-beverage customer book.
In August, Fura acquired Vancouver, Washington–based High Rise Logistics , which specializes in flatbed, expedited, TL and less-than-truckload transportation. It acquired LG Logistics Solutions — a TL, LTL and intermodal 3PL — in June.
“Fura gives our team the technology and scale to continue growing while preserving the exceptional level of service and personal connections our customers count on,” said Steve Micheli, co-founder of Road Dog.
Why it matters? Fura is demonstrating a repeatable model for consolidating the highly fragmented freight brokerage industry. Rather than simply stacking businesses and inheriting their overhead costs, Fura is migrating acquisitions onto a shared AI-powered automation platform to drive lean operations and efficiency.

Seaman Tucker Thomas looks through binoculars while standing lookout on the bridge wing of the Ticonderoga class guided-missile cruiser USS San Jacinto (CG 56) in the Mediterranean Sea, Jan. 7, 2022. (U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Conner Foy)
MILAN — For the first time in a decade, no major Russian military vessels plied the waters of the Mediterranean for several weeks earlier this year, according to a NATO official, which could signal that Moscow’s maritime forces are stretched.
NATO has tracked a “significant decrease in Russian naval presence” in the strategic body of water, so much so that until early September, “there was a two-month gap with no Russian naval presence in the Mediterranean,” said the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “The last time we saw a lack of any Russian presence there, specifically grey hulls or naval military vessels, was in 2016.”
The military official and two analysts told Breaking Defense that the reasons for the absence are myriad, ranging from the loss of access to a key Mediterranean base to the demands of protecting so-called “ shadow fleet ” vessels elsewhere.
Last year, Syria’s incoming government terminated Russia’s lease on the strategic port of Tartus, which directly weakened Moscow’s naval access to a nearby replenishment base. (A deal struck in August allows military facilities at Tartus and the coastal Hmeimem air base to be used as “joint training” centers for Russian and Syrian forces, according to The Associated Press.)
The NATO official also said the Russian Navy does not currently have a capable fleet of oilers or support vessels needed to sustain a substantial number of deployed forces over the long term.
“An example of this is that the Russian Navy has been positioning frigates in the English Channel continuously and in order to keep those supplied, they have been relying on an Amur-class repair ship designed to deliver parts or fix things on the ship — not as a replenishment one,” the official said. “So they have been forced to do hull-to-hull transfers, which are really dangerous.”
The alliance has also seen a “trend” of Kremlin military warships “escorting merchant vessels through the Baltic Sea and other areas around the Euro-Atlantic region, including the North and Mediterranean Seas,” the official added.
“These escorting activities take up valuable days at sea for the Russian Navy, and it places strain on their ability to generate naval forces for other missions,” the representative told Breaking Defense.
Basil Germond, a professor of international security at Lancaster University and a visiting fellow at the Royal Navy Strategic Studies Centre, agreed that Russia’s limited surface-combatant capacity appears to have been “increasingly being re-prioritized” to guard strategically important merchant vessels, including shadow fleet ones. He found that this reduces the number of warships readily available for a sustained Mediterranean presence .
Germond also pointed to restrictions imposed by Turkey on the transit of belligerent naval vessels through the Turkish Straits. That, he said, “prevents Russia from using the Black Sea Fleet to rotate vessels routinely into the Mediterranean,” and that the extended passage around Europe increases logistical demands.
Another expert, Federico Borsari, a fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis, concurred with the pattern NATO identified. However, he pointed out that the overall state of the Russian Navy “is one of progressive decline” in terms of capabilities and operational availability, due in part to attrition from the war in Ukraine. Operational availability issues, specifically, are “almost exclusively to the Black Sea Fleet,” while the other fleets remain “almost untouched by the war.”
And as Russian vessels returned to the Mediterranean last month, Germond said it would be unwise for NATO to think Moscow was abandoning the critical sea routes there.
“In the longer-term, [however] Russia retains both the strategic interest and the residual capability to send warships into the Mediterranean — the current situation is neither a permanent shift nor a temporary anomaly; it is an outcome of the strategic and operational reality facing the Russian Navy,” he said.

Acura's Road to 200,000 Yearly Sales in the US Includes RDX Hybrid and Two Larger SUVs

Photo: Acura
Honda's luxury-oriented marque has stopped asking the MDX to be three different SUVs. Building on a press release from a week ago, Automotive News understands that Acura wants two launch three new sport utility vehicles in the coming years with the sole purpose of hitting 200,000 annual US sales by 2030.
The product plan includes a sub-MDX crossover, namely the long-awaited RDX with hybrid assistance, as well as two larger models that will complement the MDX. An eight-seater would serve as the flagship, whereas a Honda Passport-derived sport utility vehicle would give customers a more rugged alternative to the MDX.
Based on details shared during an October 13 dealer meeting in Las Vegas, the upcoming models were presented to retailers behind closed doors. Considering that prospective MDX customers are already looking at the Lexus GX as an alternative, those new models are dearly needed as soon as possible.
Worse still for Acura, the Toyota-controlled marque also has the RX for two-row customers who prioritize comfort and the TX for three-row customers. Because of its 250-series Land Cruiser underpinnings, the GX is the kind of SUV that combines ride comfort, luxury, and off-road capability into a very cohesive overall package.
The eight-seat flagship would address the Lexus TX, and the newcomer allegedly carries the Acura XL moniker internally. Six inches (a little over 150 millimeters) longer than the MDX, the XL targets in the ballpark of 30,000 deliveries annually. Said estimate comes from supply chain sources, with production targeted for the third quarter of 2029. Otherwise put, look forward to a 2030 model.
Photo: Acura Dealers report a boxy, tall vehicle with broad shoulders, a passenger-first cabin, and a front light bar. They also drew comparisons with Range Rover products, which is great news if Acura can actually pull such a stylistic effort off without integrating some oddities in the design. Under the skin, its platform is referred to as Pilot XXL internally.
The vehicle architecture should also underpin the next MDX and a larger Honda sport utility vehicle, also with three rows and eight seats at most. As for the midsizer derived from the Passport, retailers described unique sheetmetal that includes an upright nose, all-terrain rubber, and unique hood treatment. Due in the first half of 2028, the gas-powered model is projected to sell 25,000 units annually.
Whether buyers will accept the Passport with different badging, nicer body panels, and a snazzier cabin at a higher price than the actual Passport, only time will tell. The RDX, thankfully, has a different assignment. Its role is to keep Acura competitive in existing territory, and due to the RAV4 and CR-V, the next RDX needs a hybrid option.
Confirmed to come to market in 2028, which probably means a 2029 model by US automotive standards, the fourth-gen RDX is coming with two-motor hybrid tech. Instead of a V6 hybrid setup, which is reserved for larger models, this one is certain to use an I4.
The Acura Nexera Vision concept previews the stylistic direction of all three models, blade-like lighting inspired by the A emblem included. Although a coupe design study is good enough to supply the stylistic inspiration, a crossover will do the selling in this SUV- and truck-driven market.

A view of the Steenkampskraal processing facilities. Credit: Steenkampskraal monazite mine.
Posted By: Colin McClelland October 20, 2026
South Africa’s Steenkampskraal mine is targeting its first rare earth concentrate exports before year-end following the opening of a processing plant, while plans to produce higher-value separated oxides locally remain at the development stage.
The Western Cape deposit grades about 14.5% total rare earth oxides, Mintek, the country’s state-owned minerals research organization, said on Tuesday. The first-stage plant will crush and mill ore, then use gravity separation and flotation to produce monazite concentrate for export, the research group said in a release.
“Moving from a mineral resource to a high-purity product requires much more than mining,” Mintek CEO Molefi Motuku said. “It requires the ability to understand the mineral, develop and optimise processing technologies, solve metallurgical challenges and ultimately produce a product that has commercial value.”
The development tests South Africa’s ambition to capture more value from its mineral resources through domestic processing. Steenkampskraal’s initial export product will still require further treatment, with two subsequent stages envisaged to produce a mixed rare earth product and then separate individual rare earth oxides.
Output
Mintek described the Oct. 6 opening as the start of commercial concentrate production while identifying successful commissioning and the production of saleable concentrate as immediate priorities. Its release provided no production volumes, named buyers or shipment destinations.
Mintek referred emailed questions from The Northern Miner to the Steenkampskraal mine, whose spokesperson was away sick on Tuesday and unable to immediately reply.
The mine’s owners include Steenkampskraal Holdings and Bora Mining Investments, according to the company’s website . Bora’s investment helped restart work at the site in 2024.
Processing ambitions
Mintek and Steenkampskraal produced a high-purity mixed rare earth oxalate-carbonate product at Mintek’s laboratories in June, demonstrating a potential route beyond concentration.
The next development stage would involve cracking monazite — breaking down the mineral chemically — to produce a mixed rare earth product. A third stage would separate individual rare earth oxides. Mintek says it has already piloted solvent-extraction technology for that separation.
The release gave no construction timetable or cost for either downstream stage. Laboratory results and pilot work provide a technical foundation, but commercial-scale processing remains to be established.
Thorium
Rare earths include elements used in powerful permanent magnets for electric motors and wind turbines. Steenkampskraal also contains thorium, a radioactive material that requires regulated handling and storage.
The mine opened in 1952 to produce thorium and was later placed on care and maintenance until 2024. Partial funding for the processing plant has been secured through South Africa’s Industrial Development Corporation, Mintek said.
“The objective is not simply to prove that a mineral can be processed in a laboratory,” Motuku said. “The objective is to develop technologies that can ultimately support industry.”

2028 Bentley Supersports Convertible Spied With Coupe Brother's Aerodynamic Upgrades
53 photos
Photo: SH Proshots
Following the introduction of the Supersports coupe for model year 2027, the go-faster Continental story will continue in 2027 with a convertible. Likely scheduled for production as a 2028 model, the open-top derivative was caught at the Nurburgring with little in the way of camouflage.
Dressed in matte black and carrying similar aerodynamic updates, the Supersports Convertible is anything but a Continental GTC with a bad attitude. Starting from its rear end, a very telling decklid spoiler is joined by a serious-looking aerodynamic diffuser. Being a V8, it should come as no surprise that four exhaust outlets are on the menu.
From the rear end alone, there is little attempt to soften the high-performance treatment for someone who merely wants to enjoy open-top driving. Its matte-finish body panels are complemented by Pirelli-fied black wheels, keeping the prototype's look consistent. Sill extensions and purposeful side bumper sculpting also indicate how different the Supersports is from the Continental.
As far as width is concerned, the coupe had its rear track widened by 16 millimeters (0.6 inches) because the Supersports drops all-wheel drive and plug-in hybrid nonsense for a purer drivetrain. The rear-drive special edition also benefits from rear-wheel steering and an electronically controlled limited-slip rear differential, a recipe that carries over to the convertible.
A distinctive grille, bumper, and a quarter of dive planes dominate the front end. Those small blades at the sides of the front bumper are designed to reduce front lift, whereas the outer front bumper intakes satisfy engine and brake cooling requirements. Compared to the far more discreet Continental GTC, that's a whole lot of front-end furniture.
Photo: Baldauf While it's not clear if Bentley can mirror the coupe's downforce levels, stability at speed is the name of the game here. Carrying more than a token lip beneath its nose, the prototype also prides itself on carbon-ceramic brakes. Don't expect anything other than a familiar V8 underhood, namely the 4.0-liter unit we already know from the Conti.
In this gasoline-only application, it produces a devilish 666 metric horsepower and 800 Newton-meters of twist. Make that 657 mechanical ponies and 590 pound-feet on the right octane, with most of that fury channeled to the rear axle by a dual-clutch tranny.
Breathing out through an Akrapovic lightweight exhaust system, the Supersports coupe weighs 1,998 kilograms (4,405 pounds) in European flavor. Bentley achieved this by deleting a lot of stuff, creating a more purist driving experience in the process. With the convertible's roof arrangement, matching that figure would be a substantial undertaking.
Be it similar in weight or heavier, the Supersports Convertible will undoubtedly hit 100 kph (62 mph) in less than four seconds when equipped with the stickiest of tires. Maximum speed? As long as the roof is up, expect no more than 320 kilometers per hour (199 miles per hour).

context_references.quote: How new capacity is raising rates in chaotic ocean market

source_document.body:
A South Korean container ship has completed that country’s first commercial round-trip to Europe through the Arctic , demonstrating a potentially faster alternative to the Suez Canal while leaving unresolved questions about costs, reliability and geopolitical risk.
The PanStar Acro returned to Busan on Oct. 11, completing a 50-day voyage that began Aug. 22. It sailed along Russia’s Arctic coast to Felixstowe in the United Kingdom, then called at Rotterdam and Gdansk before returning through the northern passage, Reuters reported.
The government-backed trial carried billed export cargo. South Korean officials intend to use the operational data to assess whether the route can support regular commercial services, which they hope to launch by 2030.
Shorter passage offers strategic potential
The PanStar Acro reached Felixstowe in about 20 days, according to South Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, as reported by The Korea Herald. President Lee Jae Myung said the voyage shortened the one-way sailing time by 10 days compared with the conventional Suez Canal route.
The Northern Sea Route runs along Russia’s northern coast, offering a shorter connection between Northeast Asia and Europe. For South Korea, the potential benefits extend beyond faster deliveries. Officials see the corridor as a way to diversify export-import logistics networks and strengthen Busan’s position as an international maritime hub.
The Oceans and Fisheries Ministry plans to analyze the voyage’s results before preparing further trials and commercial operations. It also sees opportunities for related shipping, shipbuilding, port and logistics businesses as part of a longer-term Arctic development strategy.
The ship sailed with just 737 loaded TEUs of a planned 1,300-TEU cargo.
In September–October 2025, the container ship Istanbul Bridge conducted a China-Europe Arctic Express trial, departing Ningbo-Zhoushan on Sept. 23 and reaching Felixstowe in about 20 days. Maersk (OTC: AMKBY ) also conducted a 2018 Arctic container-ship trial.
Analysts say that commercial viability will depend on schedule reliability, the cost of slowing or diverting to avoid ice, special insurance premiums and additional fuel consumption. Those factors could offset some of the advantages of a shorter sailing distance.
Seasonality is another limitation. The Northern Sea Route is generally more accessible during warmer months as sea ice retreats, but conditions remain unpredictable and some ships require icebreaker assistance.
The Arctic passage also introduces geopolitical complications. Because it follows Russia’s coastline, South Korea consulted Moscow about the voyage, including potential assistance if the vessel encountered ice-related problems. Reuters reported that expanded cooperation could create friction with Western allies seeking to isolate Russia over its war in Ukraine.
Environmental advocates have also warned that greater commercial traffic could damage fragile Arctic ecosystems and accelerate ice loss. The initiative points up the tension between exploiting a route made more accessible by warming temperatures and protecting the region.

source_document.body:
PARIS — China built more than twice the naval tonnage of the United States in the 2024-25 period, narrowing the gap between the two countries’ navies, according to the World Defense Shipbuilding report published by Euronaval ahead of the 2026 edition of the naval defense show.
The combined tonnage of combat ships built by China in the two years through to December 2025 amounted to 636,208 tons, compared to 270,509 tons for the United States, according to data compiled by Flottes de Combat and French maritime industry association Gican.
China accounted for more than a third of the global naval tonnage constructed in 2024-25, based on the Euronaval report. U.S. lawmakers and congressional researchers have warned that China’s greater shipbuilding capacity, combined with delays and bottlenecks in U.S. naval shipbuilding, could hurt America’s ability to keep up with Beijing’s expanding fleet.
“We are seeing a fairly substantial expansion of naval forces, and consequently of shipbuilding,” said Philippe Missoffe, the general director of Gican, in a press briefing here on Tuesday. “We’re seeing an increase in power capabilities, particularly nuclear-powered attack submarines for example.”
Global naval construction overall was booming in the period, with 1.47 million tons of combat vessels built in 2024-25, compared with 959,671 tons in the prior two years. The value of global naval construction amounted to $123.9 billion, climbing from $81.8 billion in 2022-23.
The value of Chinese combat-vessel construction was US$43.5 billion in the latest two-year period, compared with $26.8 billion for the U.S., the report said.
China has reversed roles from 2022-2023, when production of the country’s naval yards amounted to 202,520 tons, compared with 245,703 tons for the U.S., according to the previous edition of the shipbuilding report published in 2024.
The U.S. fleet of combat vessels of more than 200 tons amounted to 3.11 million tons as of Jan. 1, 2026, compared to 1.44 million tons for China’s fleet, the report showed, That compares with 3.22 million tons for the U.S. and 1.3 million tons for China two years earlier.
Russia was in third place in terms of naval construction in 2024-25, with 149,056 tons built, followed by India with 76,430 tons and Italy with 53,700 tons. Turkey, France, Japan, South Korean and Romania rounded out the top 10 of naval builders.
The four-day Euronaval show, the world’s biggest maritime-defense exhibition, is set to kick of in Paris on Nov. 3. The number of exhibitors will be more than 40% higher than in 2024, according to the organizers.

Volvo EX30 and EX30 Cross Country EVs Recalled for Detaching Head Restraint Cushions
14 photos
Photo: Volvo
There's no mistaking that Volvo built its reputation on protecting occupants in crash scenarios. A recall about a head restraint cushion, therefore, certainly deserves attention. The Swedish automaker is recalling a grand total of 9,930 vehicles over this concern, with Volvo Car USA highlighting that said cushions may come off during severe crashes.
Does a headrest cushion make a world of difference in a severe crash? Volvo says it does, for it provides vital support to the occupant's head exactly when maximum support is required. The NHTSA calls this campaign 26V671 and lists two model years, namely 2025 and 2026, with production dates ranging from March 3, 2023, all the way through August 28, 2026.
Although the cushion per se is not defective, attachment strength isn't good enough. Volvo's investigation determined that certain head restraint cushions are likely to come off because of insufficient fastening. The recall filing describes the crash that exposes the fastening issue, specifically high-speed scenarios combined with impacts from multiple directions.
That particular combination of variables increases the risk of a cushion separating from the head restraint structure. Thankfully for Volvo's legal team and customers alike, Volvo Car USA is not aware of any report alleging injuries (or worse) connected with the recall condition.
Not as fortunate, the recall condition offers no warning before a crash. The head restraint and its cushion look and function just as intended in everyday use, with the defect revealing itself only when the battery-electric vehicle is subjected to the multi-directional loading that severe crashes produce. China-based Magna Seating Baoji is listed as the supplier of the cushion.
Photo: Volvo Volvo started looking into this problem back in September 2025. Both the automaker and the supplier began separate investigations, assessing the existing design to come up with a more robust revision. One year later, Volvo classified the problem as critical, deciding to prepare a recall after identifying the safety risks associated with a detaching cushion.
Rather than replacing the entire head restraint or seat, service technicians are to apply two-component epoxy adhesive at three attachment points using the specified tools. Physical testing confirmed the improvement in attachment strength, and truth be told, some epoxy adhesive here and there is the best-case scenario for Volvo from the standpoint of repair costs.
YV12YEL03V2615920 is featured in the recall documentation as the last vehicle built with the old cushion design. Volvo retailers have already been instructed, whereas customer notifications are in the offing for November 30, 2026. Affected vehicle identification numbers are now searchable on the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's website.
Currently the smallest electric Volvo sport utility vehicle of them all, the EX30 is a strict five-seater that can be had in single- and twin-motor flavors. To be discontinued in the US market after model year 2026 due to tariffs, poor demand, the loss of incentives, and a general feeling of uncertainty, the EX40's brother now retails at $40,345 for its most basic of specs.
Highlights include up to 422 horsepower, 3.4 seconds to 60 mph (97 kph), less than half an hour to recharge from 10 to 80 percent, and 261 miles (420 kilometers) on a full charge. The Cross Country version of the EX30 is ruggedized, targeting buyers who need additional ground clearance to suit their outdoorsy lifestyles.

Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO October 20, 2026
Heliostar Metals (TSX: HSTR; US-OTC: HSTXF) has intersected gold below the planned workings of its Ana Paula project in Mexico, pointing to expansion potential as it prepares a feasibility study for an underground mine producing about 100,000 oz. a year.
Hole AP-26-411 in the Expansion Zone cut 8 metres grading 6.88 grams gold per tonne from 469 metres depth, Heliostar said Monday . Nearby hole AP-26-314A returned 9.7 metres grading 4.33 grams gold per tonne from 598.6 metres downhole.
“Infill results at the High-Grade Panel continue to show remarkably consistent mineralization, while large step-outs at the Expansion zone continue to point to growth beyond the scope of the upcoming feasibility study,” ATB Cormark mining analyst Richard Gray said Tuesday in a note.
Heliostar is preparing a feasibility study expected in the second quarter of 2027, followed by a potential construction decision in mid-2027. The company is advancing Ana Paula as an underground operation, replacing an earlier open-pit development concept for which environmental approval was granted in 2017. First gold production is targeted by the end of 2028.
Drilling shows that the Expansion Zone remains open to the south, west and at depth, providing additional targets for exploration.
Infill drilling
Hole AP-26-405 in the High-Grade Panel zone cut 52.4 metres grading 5.84 grams gold per tonne from 46.9 metres downhole, including 12.6 metres of 17.8 grams gold from 76.4 metres, Heliostar said. Hole AP-26-407 cut 24.8 metres grading 5.14 grams gold per tonne from 43 metres.
Both holes were part of an infill program designed to improve confidence in the central portion of the deposit and support its inclusion in a mine plan.
Crews have drilled 122 holes totalling 35,121 metres in the company’s 2025-26 exploration program. About 25,000 metres targeted inferred resources for potential conversion to higher-confidence categories, while 10,000 metres tested extensions beyond the mine plan.
Nine-year life
Heliostar’s current development plan for Ana Paula is based on a preliminary economic assessment released last November. It targets a nine-year mine life. Initial capital was estimated at $300 million (C$420 million).
At a $3,800 per oz. gold price and a 5% discount rate, the project has an after-tax net present value of about $1 billion and a 51% internal rate of return with a 1.9-year payback period. Ana Paula is located about 180 km southwest of Mexico City.
Heliostar acquired the property from Argonaut Gold in March 2023 for $10 million in cash, after previous owners had invested more than $100 million in exploration and development. The company subsequently shifted its focus to the deposit’s higher-grade underground mineralization.
Ana Paula is Heliostar’s most advanced project. It’s one of several assets in Mexico and the United States that the Vancouver-based miner is looking to develop as it targets production of 500,000 oz. per year by the end of the decade. Development work is being financed by cash flow from the company’s two Mexican mines, La Colorada in Sonora state and San Agustin in Durango.
Heliostar shares rose 1.6% to C$2.72 late Tuesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$705 million ($504 million). The stock has traded between C$1.54 and C$3.47 in the past year.

Container shipping lines are pushing freight rates higher even as a gradual return to the Red Sea promises to release capacity into a softening market, as competing forces shape ocean freight heading into 2027.
The recovery in Suez Canal routings is unfolding despite persistent security risks in the Middle East, said analyst and SONAR data contributor Freightos (NASDAQ: CRGO ). Meanwhile, increased vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has coincided with more Iranian attacks, as some operators resume passage through threatened waterways.
Iranian attacks on ships crossing Hormuz have surged as Persian Gulf oil flows recovered toward prewar levels, Bloomberg reported. As of its Oct. 13 report, however, there was no clear evidence of a corresponding reduction in oil loadings among several major regional producers.
Iranian forces sank a Dubai-linked container vessel this past week, demonstrating that some container operators are also accepting the risks of transiting Hormuz, although tankers still account for most traffic. Crude prices remain around $100 per barrel despite the recovery in exports, reflecting continued concern over potential supply disruptions.
In the Red Sea, escalating violence between Yemen-based Houthi rebels and the Saudis have added to concerns about the security of shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the route’s southern end. Nevertheless, container lines are steadily restoring services through the Suez Canal after the widespread diversions that began in late 2023.
Maersk (OTC: AMKBY ) and Hapag-Lloyd’s Gemini Cooperation expects to return nearly all its services to Suez routings during the first quarter of 2027, provided conditions do not change, Hapag-Lloyd Chief Executive Rolf Habben Jansen said recent public comments.
The partners plan to introduce another Asia-Mediterranean service through Suez in November. The service, designated AE18 by Maersk and SE5 by Hapag-Lloyd, will connect Chinese ports with western Mediterranean transshipment hubs, with its first sailing scheduled to leave Shanghai on Nov. 22.
Liner analyst Lars Jensen estimated that Suez routing had returned to roughly 30% to 35% of normal across the market, with the recovery slightly further advanced on backhaul voyages than on headhaul sailings. He described the measured pace as a positive surprise, reducing the risk of an abrupt network transition.
High fuel costs and port congestion may help explain carriers’ willingness to return from longer diverted routings around Africa despite the security threats. It also points to evolving geopolitical calculations, including the possibility that the Houthis could avoid commercial shipping while directing greater pressure toward Riyadh.
The phased return should help ports manage the arrival of ships completing shorter voyages, limiting the vessel bunching and schedule disruption that could accompany a sudden, industrywide shift.
Habben Jansen said Gemini’s step-by-step approach had allowed it to manage workloads at European and Mediterranean hubs without major problems so far.
In a potential benefit to shippers, the restoration follows the early-July Asia-Europe demand peak and will continue through lower-demand months, reducing the potential disruption compared with a peak-season transition.
Port congestion continues to absorb some vessel capacity, although backlogs at major Asia hubs are easing. That provides a partial counterweight to the capacity released as ships circulate more quickly through the Red Sea.
Over time, however, shorter voyages would increase effective fleet capacity, adding to the risk of excess supply in 2027 if demand fails to keep pace.
Trans-Pacific rates were largely unchanged in the past week but remained elevated, according to the Freightos Baltic Index. Asia-U.S. West Coast prices stood at $8,126 per FEU, while East Coast rates increased 1% to $9,700 per FEU.
On the Asia-Europe trades, carriers have secured some spot-rate gains despite weakening demand and the gradual release of capacity.
Asia-North Europe rates rose 6% last week to $3,442 per forty-foot equivalent unit, while Asia-Mediterranean rates increased 3% to $3,927 per FEU.
The increases follow recent general rate increases aimed at strengthening pricing as negotiations for 2027 long-term contracts begin. Some forwarders remain skeptical that the gains will hold given current supply-and-demand conditions.
Daily readings early this week indicated further upward pressure despite expectations that volumes are cooling. Capacity reductions as the trade enters its slower season may be helping support prices.
On the trans-Atlantic, announced October increases have produced more modest gains. Spot rates have risen about $200 per FEU since the end of September to approximately $2,850 per FEU.
That leaves trans-Atlantic prices about 25% above year-earlier levels, potentially reflecting pressure from elevated bunker costs, even as carriers struggle to implement the full increases they sought.

After months of volatility, the diesel market going into Tuesday appeared to have calmed down, at least for now.
The day also featured the release of the weekly benchmark diesel price from the Department of Energy/Energy Information Administration that is used for most fuel surcharges. After a big one-day increase last week in the price of ultra low sulfur diesel traded on the CME commodity exchange, the DOE/EIA price followed suit, rising 9.7 cents/gallon this week to $6.276/g.
The price is effective Monday but released Tuesday.
This week’s DOE/EIA price is still about 25 cts/g less than the all-time high of $6.529/g, set on September 22. There had been three weeks of declines since that day before this week’s increase.
Over in the futures market, ultra low sulfur diesel (ULSD) on the CME commodity exchange during the last few days had hit something of a lull.
After the big increase of more than 21 cts/g on Tuesday, October 13, which was a reaction primarily to the market realization that short-term steps like the Trump administration diesel deal with Russia were going to have limited to no impact, the ULSD market at approximately 10:30 a.m. EDT Tuesday was not far from where it settled on October 13.
The 10/13 settle was $4.9344/g. Mid-morning Tuesday, ULSD was at $4.9457/g.
And then a quick move downward
But it didn’t take long for volatility to return. Soon after those numbers were recorded, oil prices took a sharp move to the downside.
The reason? What multiple news outlets said were “unconfirmed” reports that Qatar and Pakistan together had proposed to kick start new talks aimed at ending the Iran war.
Those reports actually circulated Monday. They seemed to give a new downward push to oil markets Tuesday.
The moves were a testament to a market that is so on edge that even unconfirmed reports that two nations who aren’t directly involved in the Middle East conflict were talking about trying to get a peace process going was enough to push prices lower.
Most of the external news that might impact markets in the last week had increasingly been discounted by markets.
There have not been enough differing news reports to suggest either an increasing or decreasing amount of oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz.
As noted, the Russian diesel plan, while politically controversial in the U.S., is not seen as providing any sort of significant alteration to the supply/demand balance.
Crack spread normalizes
Even the crack spread between Brent and ULSD has settled into a relatively narrow range. A comparison of first month Brent versus second month ULSD on CME has mostly been in a range of 83 to 88 cts/gallon for about a month, with the occasional pop over 90 cts/g. That relatively stability is mostly a sign that the Brent market and ULSD’s relationship is still one of diesel stronger than historic differentials, but where the spread has stopped blowing out.
One development that shouldn’t have an impact on prices: a lockout at the Phillips 66 Bayway refiner in New Jersey.
According to news reports, Phillips 66 locked out members of the Teamsters Monday afternoon following the expiration of their contract.
Operations at the refinery are said to be continuing normally. Unlike a lockout or strike at something like an automobile plant, a refinery can continue to run normally for an indeterminate time before the lack of a work force impacts operations.

Truckload carrier Heartland Express booked its first net profit since 2023 without the help of outsized gains from equipment and terminal sales.
The North Liberty, Iowa-based company reported third-quarter revenue of $179.5 million, a 9% year-over-year decline and below the $191.4 million consensus estimate. (Revenue was 15% lower y/y, excluding fuel surcharges.)
Net income of $1 million (1 cent per share) was a turnaround from an $8.3 million loss (11 cents per share) in the year-ago quarter . Analysts were calling for EPS of 3 cents in the period. (Higher gains on sale were a 1-cent y/y EPS tailwind.)
“The improved financial results reflect stronger freight volumes and improved customer pricing resulting from ongoing industry capacity reductions, even though we do not expect the positive impacts of ongoing contract negotiations to be fully reflected in our operating results until 2027,” said CEO Mike Gerdin in a news release.
Heartland ( NASDAQ: HTLD ) does not host a quarterly call, nor does it provide operating metrics for utilization and pricing.
Table: Heartland’s key performance indicators
The company booked a 97.6% adjusted operating ratio (operating expenses expressed as a percentage of revenue), which was 590 basis points better y/y. It called out cost pressures such as fuel, maintenance and repairs, and employee-related expenses during the period.
SONAR: Outbound Tender Rejection Index (OTRI.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). A proxy for truck capacity, the tender rejection index shows the number of loads being rejected by carriers. Current tender rejections show a tight truckload market. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
SONAR: Van Contract Rate Per Mile Index ( VCRPM1.USA ) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). The index shows a 7-day moving average of the initial reporting of dry van contract rates without fuel or accessorial charges.
Operating cash flows totaled $55 million for the first nine months of 2026. The company continues to replace equipment, pay a cash dividend and repurchase stock. An average tractor age of 2.3 years was down from 2.6 years in the year-ago quarter.
Heartland has nearly paid off its debt since leveraging up to acquire a pair of carriers in the summer of 2022. During the third quarter, it reduced net debt by $21 million to $73 million. It ended the period with $89 million available on an untapped revolving credit facility and was in compliance with financial covenants.
Shares of HTLD were off 0.6% at 12:08 p.m. EDT on Tuesday compared to the S&P 500, which was up 0.4%.
Why it matters? Heartland’s return to profitability through stronger freight volumes and improved pricing rather than asset sales signals that capacity reductions are successfully restoring core operating fundamentals.

source_document.body:
Spain's former foregin minister Ana Palacio urged strong EU support for mining to mirror American policy. Credit: The Northern Miner.
By: Colin McClelland in Seville October 20, 2026
Europe needs to match its critical minerals ambitions with purchase guarantees, public investment and stable policies if it wants companies to build mines and processing plants, speakers told the sixth Mining and Minerals Hall conference in Seville on Tuesday.
The European Union has set 2030 benchmarks for domestic capacity to extract the equivalent of at least 10% of its annual strategic raw materials consumption, process 40% and recycle 25%. Delivering that capacity will require governments to share investment risks and strengthen the industrial chain beyond extraction, panellists said.
“Mining needs stability, and the problem that we have in Europe is that we don’t guarantee stability,” former Spanish foreign minister Ana Palacio said. “We need big pacts, big agreements where everybody commits.”
The challenge extends beyond shortening permit timelines. Europe must make projects commercially attractive while overcoming weak exploration spending, processing limitations and shortages of skilled workers. Otherwise, greater mineral production could leave its dependence on foreign processors largely intact.
The three-day conference , organized by Spanish metallic mining association Aminer and promoted by Andalusia’s regional government, brings together 332 exhibitors and about 100 speakers. It runs through Thursday at Seville’s Fibes conference centre.
Palacio urged Europe to learn from the U.S.’s use of tax credits and purchase guarantees to support strategically important production. European governments also need to strengthen their internal market and make their capital markets more attractive to domestic savers, she said.
“We don’t have easy tools, but the U.S. have all the easiness that Europe doesn’t have,” Palacio said. “Let’s learn from them, truly.”
Washington’s approach includes direct support for prices and customers. MP Materials (NYSE: MP) announced a 10-year price-floor agreement with the U.S. Department of Defense in July 2025 for its neodymium-praseodymium products, alongside an agreement covering magnet purchases from a planned factory.
Europe is developing its own measures. The European Commission’s RESourceEU plan , announced in December, proposed a critical raw materials centre to help coordinate investment and secure supplies, alongside joint purchasing and offtake agreements.
Andalusian President Juan Manuel Moreno Bonilla highlighted two projects designated strategic by the European Commission during the opening ceremony: Atlantic Copper’s newly launched CirCular electronics-recycling plant and Cobre Las Cruces’ planned polymetallic development. Both form part of the region’s effort to capture more value through processing and recycling alongside extraction.
Public authorities must change the investment equation where markets won’t shoulder the risks, Mark Rachovides, president emeritus of European mining industry association Euromines, said.
“Sometimes we need to use that dirty word subsidies. That’s what the Americans are doing,” he said. “They are subsidizing their producers for long-term gain.”
Beyond permits
Spain’s deputy director general for mines, Daniel Torrejón Braojos, cautioned that legislation cannot quickly deliver projects that require years of exploration, engineering and investment.
“Mining projects need time because they have long periods of maturing,” he said. “There’s no magical solution from one day to the other. You cannot open a mine.”
Torrejón challenged the idea that permitting alone explains Europe’s limited mining development. Governments also need exploration programs that improve knowledge of their resources and encourage companies to pursue discoveries.
The European Commission’s 2023 impact assessment found that the EU accounted for only about 2% to 3% of worldwide exploration expenditure between 2010 and 2022. It also identified energy costs as a key factor determining where processing and refining take place.
Torrejón pointed to another weakness: producing copper concentrate in Spain does not ensure the country captures the subsequent processing business. Technologies that allow complex concentrates to be treated domestically are also needed, he said.
Andalusia’s mining director general, Jesús Portillo García-Pintos, said regional authorities could contribute through geological research, data sharing and better coordination with national governments. But regional efforts to accelerate approvals remain constrained by national and European legislation.
Europe also needs to recognize the limits of its mineral endowment and maintain strong trading relationships, he said.
“Europe has what it has. We don’t have more than what we have,” Portillo said. “That’s important to be aware of.”
Chile’s Mining Chamber President Manuel Viera offered a similar warning from an established producing country.
“Having a resource doesn’t guarantee that we have the value chain,” he said.
Declining copper grades require more material to be processed, increasing costs and the need for technology, Viera said. He encouraged partnerships between Chilean resource owners and European processing and technology companies.
Old waste, new metals
Europe could also recover more materials from historical mining and industrial sites, Rachovides said. Modern processes can extract metals that earlier operators did not value or could not recover economically.
“You can also use technology today, which wasn’t available in the past, to get better extraction from materials,” he said. “So that means, for example, remining an old copper site, remining an old polymetallic site to extract things that weren’t valued at the time.”
Such projects could combine production with rehabilitation and employment, but still need a viable investment case, he said.
Public acceptance also requires more than explaining the demand for metals. Communities need confidence in how projects operate, Portillo said.
“Trust can only be based on transparency,” he said. “Society will trust us if we are sufficiently transparent to show what we do, why we do it, and how we do it.”

source_document.body:
I’ve tested e-bikes that cost $10,000. I’ve tested e-bikes that cost $500. But until recently, I’d never tested a brand-new e-bike that cost less than a nice set of bicycle tires.
So when I stumbled across a $199 e-bike for sale through Walmart’s website, my curiosity got the better of me.
To be clear, I wasn’t expecting it to be good. I wasn’t even really expecting it to be acceptable. This was more of a morbid curiosity experiment: What exactly does $199 buy you in the world of e-bikes?
Apparently, the answer is: more than I expected, but also fewer pedals than I expected.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The bike in question is from a brand called “Bropath”, and it’s a tiny folding e-bike with 14-inch wheels, a 350/500W rear hub motor (disparity based on which marketing blurb you read), and a surprisingly large 576Wh battery.
On paper, that’s actually fairly impressive, especially for the rock-bottom price. The bike claims a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h) and around 20 miles (32 km) of range. There’s a throttle, pedal assist, a suspension fork, mechanical disc brakes, a rear rack/basket that also houses the battery, and even a folding frame.
Things started getting interesting as soon as I pulled it out of the box, which you’ll definitely want to check out in my unboxing and testing video .
The bike was mostly assembled, but the battery basket wasn’t actually attached to the rack. There were holes where bolts clearly should have gone, but no bolts. I checked the box. I checked the packaging. I checked the instructions.
No bolts.
Eventually I resorted to temporarily ratchet-strapping the entire battery basket to the bike, which is not generally a step included in professional bicycle assembly.
Then, just as I thought I was ready for a test ride, I noticed another small problem: the bike didn’t have pedals.
Not “the pedals weren’t installed.” There simply weren’t any pedals in the box.
My guess is that an accessory box containing the pedals and battery mounting hardware was forgotten during packaging, or perhaps I received a re-packaged bike and they were left out. Fortunately, I live, eat, and breathe bikes, so my garage contains enough miscellaneous bicycle parts to make a small bike shop jealous. I eventually found two long bolts that fit the battery basket and a spare pair of pedals.
Before that, though, I did what any reasonable person would do: I rode it like a scooter with my feet resting on the bare cranks.
And that’s where things got surprising: the darn thing actually worked.
The little e-bike pulled away under throttle and moderately quickly got me cruising at nearly 20 mph (32 km/h). The brakes, which look like they were manufactured from approximately the same grade of metal as a soup can, actually stopped the bike reasonably well. The motor had decent power, the throttle worked, and once I installed pedals, the pedal assist worked too. On that note though: the single-speed design and small 14″ wheels meant that once the pedal assist kicked in, you’d quickly be going faster than your feet could keep up on the pedals. With that ghost pedaling in effect, the pedal assist quickly became useless, so don’t expect to ride this as a pedal-assist bike.
To test out the cargo capacity of the little battery basket, I took it on a shopping trip and managed to haul home several bags of groceries. I wouldn’t load it down with several cases of beer, but light duty grocery runs seems possible.
Is it a good e-bike? I wouldn’t go that far. But for $199, it was shockingly adequate. And I mean that as a compliment.
Yes, there are plenty of compromises. The suspension fork feels like a wet noodle, to the point that I’d probably rather have a rigid fork. The tiny 14-inch wheels combined with the cheap suspension make rough pavement and gravel paths fairly unpleasant. The seatpost is so short that even I can’t get a particularly good pedaling position, and I’m not exactly an NBA center.
And like I mentioned, the single-speed drivetrain also means that once the pedal assist gets you moving quickly, your legs can’t really keep up with the gearing. You wind up ghost pedaling while the motor does most of the work.
There are bigger questions, too.
I don’t know what cells are inside that 576Wh battery, and I certainly wouldn’t assume the battery has the sort of third-party safety certification I’d prefer to see on an e-bike. I don’t know how many years – or months – the suspension fork will last. I don’t know how the folding mechanism will hold up after hundreds of cycles, because it definitely doesn’t look robust.
And if something does break, you’re probably largely on your own. At this price, you’re not paying for a nationwide dealer network or a robust customer service department. This is basically a white-labeled budget e-bike, and part of the $199 experience is accepting that you will likely become your own mechanic.
That’s why I wouldn’t recommend this bike to most people.
If you can afford to spend more on a quality e-bike from an established company with better components, a certified battery, replacement parts, and real customer support, I think you should. When people ask me what the most affordable e-bike is that is still good quality, I generally send them to a $799 Lectric XP Lite-series e-bike. By the time you start upgrading parts on a bike like this $199 Walmart bike, adding likes better fork, brakes, drivetrain, or other components, you could have simply bought a better e-bike in the first place.
But there’s another side to this.
For someone who genuinely only has $200 to spend and needs transportation, this thing is transportation.
It got me to the store. It got me to lunch. It carried groceries. It cruised at nearly 20 mph. Once I supplied the missing parts myself, everything basically worked (and I assume most people will be luckier than me and get all the parts in the box).
And that’s what surprised me most.
I went into this experiment expecting a $199 e-bike to be almost comically terrible. Instead, I found something that was undeniably cheap, questionable in several places, and certainly not something I’d choose as my everyday e-bike – yet was also far more functional than it had any right to be at this price.
There’s a big difference between “good” and “good for $199.”
This bike definitely isn’t the former.
But somehow, against all odds, it might actually be the latter.

Subaru is phasing out combustion-engine vehicles in Europe by the end of 2027 and will sell only EVs.
Subaru drops gas engine for EVs in Europe
The Japanese automaker will stop selling internal combustion engine vehicles in Europe by the end of next year, at the latest.
Known for its boxer engines, Subaru’s shift to an all-electric lineup is not necessarily by choice. Subaru Germany confirmed the news to Auto Motor und sport , saying the decision is due to the European Union’s emissions and driver-assistance regulations.
The transition will start with the Outback, Subaru’s iconic wagon, which will be discontinued at the end of the year.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
In 2027, three more boxer-powered models will follow, including the Impreza, Crosstrek, and Forester, all of which use Subaru’s mild-hybrid 2.0L boxer engine.
From 2028, three EVs will remain in Subaru’s European lineup: the Solterra, E-Outback, and Uncharted. The three electric crossover SUVs are developed with Toyota and are twins of the bZ4X, bZ4X Touring, and C-HR+.
2026 Subaru Solterra (Source: Subaru Germany)
Subaru is not ruling out full hybrid drive vehicles for Europe at some point, but has no official plans yet.
The decision only applies to Europe. In the US, Subaru still sells the Crosstrek and Forester with a 2.5L full hybrid boxer engine.
2026 Subaru E-Outback (Source: Subaru Germany)
Subaru’s US electric vehicle lineup consists of the Solterra, Uncharted, and Trailseeker , which is sold as the E-Outback in Europe. Next year, it will add its first three-row electric SUV, the Getway. It’s essentially a rebadged version of Toyota’s three-row electric SUV, the Highlander BEV.
Separately, Subaru showcased its first in-house EV tech to reporters on Sunday as it plans to wean off its reliance on Toyota for its next-generation electric vehicles.
2026 Subaru Uncharted (Source: Subaru Germany)
The new tech includes Subaru’s first dedicated EV platform, plus new batteries, electric motors, and an integrated control unit to enable over-the-air updates.
Subaru didn’t reveal a specific launch date, but company officials said some of the new EV tech will begin rolling out around 2029.
The company showcased a disguised Outback test vehicle fitted with an all-wheel-drive powertrain that delivered a combined 509 horsepower (380 kW). According to Subaru, the setup is lighter, more efficient, and enables the EV to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in under 4 seconds.

As the U.S. Army’s support to the joint force space mission takes shape with its newly populated Space Operations Branch , the service is also poised to support what’s expected to be a critical year for testing and development of the Golden Dome for America (GDA) missile shield project.
Speaking with reporters at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting last week, Lt. Gen. John L. Rafferty, commanding general of U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, confirmed that an Army air defense unit had been “earmarked” for GDA support.
The unit, which he declined to identify, is “a well-trained organization that we know can meet the demands of Golden Dome for America when the systems are fielded,” Rafferty said.
With the current air defense systems across the joint force grouped in aggregated packages, including a sensor, an interceptor and a command-and-control package, Rafferty said he understood GDA as a way to do some disaggregation and bring together command-and-control systems into a group that can work together across the United States.
“So now, as you array sensors and interceptors and C2 platforms across the country, you can use any sensor, best shooter, right C2, in that disaggregated way,” he said. “So we believe that right now … we have the most experienced air defense and combat-seasoned air defense formations in the world [and] we have the right people with the right experience to manage the system when they get here, with some training.”
Joint Task Force Gold , a 100-person unit established in January under U.S. Northern Command and led by Army officers, is also leaning into preparation for Golden Dome with planning drills and stakeholder gatherings, said Col. Kevin “Stoney” Stonerook, deputy commander of the task force.
“We are helping put together the team of teams, all the different stakeholder communities, be that vendors and other government agencies, to really provide a cyber warfare capability for GDA,” Stonerook said. “We definitely know that we are involved in putting together some of the sites as we look at building out GDA across the country and other areas, and trying to integrate all those capabilities across the multiple layers of GDA, but there’s a lot we still have to figure out.”
The task force, he said, had hosted a series of planning “sprints” beginning in February, working with about 300 members of the “GDA stakeholder community” on-site in Colorado Springs to hash out a concept of operations for the project and to identify unanswered questions.
The next planning sprint, Stonerook said, was set for the end of October.
“We’re continuing to find out more and help focus the efforts of not just the JTF-Gold 100-plus personnel, but all the rest of the stakeholder communities to really focus on those questions needing to be answered for … operationalization,” he said.
President Donald Trump listens to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speak about the Golden Dome missile defense shield. (Jim Watson via Getty Images)
Pentagon officials have said they’re looking to field an early version of GDA by the end of next year — to meet a goal of having an operational shield by the end of President Donald Trump’s second term, with a more fully realized version of the system to be built out by 2035.
But lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have expressed frustration with slow progress and inconsistent communication from the White House over the way forward with the ambitious and expensive project.
The Pentagon requested $17.5 billion for Golden Dome in fiscal 2027 through a $350 billion reconciliation package, and just about $400 million for the project in research and development funds, within the base budget request. As Air and Space Forces Magazine reported in September, dispute over passage of the reconciliation bill could leave the bulk of funding in jeopardy.
At the panel with reporters, Rafferty maintained the Army was all in on supporting development of the shield system.
“I really try to draw no distinction between [Army Space and Missile Defense Command] and JTF-Gold,” he said. “It’s going to take all of us to help enable the defense of the homeland through Golden Dome for America, and it is SMDC’s No. 1 priority to protect the homeland. So we’re all in to help to deliver that.”
